title: Healthcare Data Engineering and ETL Laboratory
description: Eight practical ETL challenges covering batch ingestion, paginated APIs, data contracts, quality controls, database loading, idempotency, scheduling and client handoff.

challenges.title: ETL architecture, source inventory and data contracts
challenges.scenario: A hospital analytics team receives encounter and medication-order extracts from two systems. Before coding, define what enters the pipeline and what each record means.
tasks: Document source owner, format, refresh frequency, primary key, grain and expected row count.
Define required fields, data types, allowed nulls and key constraints.
Draw Extract → Raw → Validate → Transform → Curated Mart → Report.
Write a data contract for encounter and medication-order records.
State why a medication order is not proof of administration or dispensing.
challenges.starter:
Encounter grain: one row per encounter_id.
Medication-order grain: one row per order_id.
Required encounter key: encounter_id.
Required order key: order_id; encounter_id is a foreign reference.
challenges.hint: Do not design a table before defining its grain. One patient may have multiple encounters; one encounter may have multiple orders.
challenges.solution: Use `etl/DATA_CONTRACTS.md` and `etl/PIPELINE_ARCHITECTURE.md`. Define keys and required types, then map each transformation to a test and an owner. Record the synthetic-only restriction and data lineage.
challenges.expected: A one-page source inventory, two data contracts and a pipeline diagram with clear grains and failure paths.

challenges.title: Batch ingestion from CSV with reproducible manifests
challenges.scenario: A weekly batch of encounter and order files must be ingested reproducibly, with proof of which files were processed.
tasks: Create a virtual environment and install requirements-etl.txt.
Run the ETL script in CSV mode.
Inspect raw tables, curated marts, ETL run log, quality report and manifest.
Record source checksums and row counts.
Run the pipeline a second time and confirm the mart row counts do not grow.
challenges.starter:
Linux / Fish:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate.fish
pip install -r requirements-etl.txt
python scripts/healthcare_etl_pipeline.py --source csv

Windows PowerShell:
py -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
py -m pip install -r requirements-etl.txt
py scripts\healthcare_etl_pipeline.py --source csv
challenges.hint: Raw tables preserve source payloads; curated marts apply validation and normalisation. INSERT OR REPLACE makes the supplied key-based load repeatable for this training case.
challenges.solution: Run the commands above from the Academy root. Open `assignments/outputs/healthcare_etl_training.db` in DBeaver or SQLite. Inspect `etl_run_log`, `data_quality_results` and the manifest JSON. Run the same command again and compare table counts.
challenges.expected: 80 encounter records and 150 medication-order records in the supplied source. This source does not include unit cost, so the pipeline reports the field as not supplied rather than treating all rows as missing-cost exceptions.
acceptance: Manifest includes file hashes and counts.
Repeat run does not duplicate mart keys.

challenges.title: Paginated API extraction and resilient request design
challenges.scenario: A source API returns records in pages. A robust extractor must detect missing pages and avoid leaking credentials.
tasks: Inspect the mock API JSON pages and identify the pagination metadata.
Run the pipeline with --source mock-api.
Review the generic REST extractor template and document its expected `results` and `next` response contract.
Explain HTTPS, bearer-token environment variables, timeouts, retry/backoff, rate limits and pagination safety.
Do not call a real clinical API or put tokens in source code.
challenges.starter:
python scripts/healthcare_etl_pipeline.py --source mock-api

Generic REST environment variables:
HDA_API_BASE_URL=https://approved.example
HDA_API_ENDPOINT=/v1/encounters
HDA_API_TOKEN=<set in environment, never commit>
challenges.hint: The mock API path reads local fixture files and tests pagination completeness. The generic REST extractor is a template only; real APIs differ in authentication, paging, schemas and rate limits.
challenges.solution: Use `etl/mock_api/` to inspect page numbers, total_records and next_page. The pipeline verifies page order and total record count. `scripts/healthcare_api_extractor_template.py` demonstrates a separate full-next-URL pattern with HTTPS enforcement, environment-based bearer token, timeouts and retries. Adapt only after confirming the real API contract.
challenges.expected: Mock API route extracts 80 encounters and 150 orders. No network request is required or performed by the Academy pipeline.
acceptance: Credentials absent from source and logs.
Retry, timeout and rate-limit behaviour explained.

challenges.title: Data quality rules, quarantine and failure handling
challenges.scenario: A medication-order record references an encounter that does not exist. The pipeline must retain evidence and prevent it from silently entering the curated mart.
tasks: Review required-key, uniqueness, date, quantity and foreign-reference rules.
Inject a deliberately invalid encounter reference into a copy of the source file.
Run the pipeline and inspect quarantine_orders.
Compare raw row count, curated row count and quarantined count.
Decide which issues are fatal errors versus warnings.
challenges.starter:
Validation dimensions:
Completeness: required fields present
Uniqueness: primary key unique
Validity: dates parse; quantity > 0
Referential integrity: order.encounter_id exists in encounters
Timeliness: source extract timestamp is current
challenges.hint: Do not delete a bad row without retaining its source payload and rejection reason. A warning does not necessarily block the whole batch; a broken primary key or invalid date may.
challenges.solution: Use the ETL01 invalid-reference scenario. The supplied script preserves raw data and quarantines orphan orders with reason `orphan_encounter_reference`. It does not load them into the curated order mart. `--fail-on-errors` blocks the run when ERROR-severity rules are violated.
challenges.expected: In the supplied clean source: 80 encounters, 150 orders, no orphan records. In the injected test: 1 order quarantined and 149 orders loaded to the mart.
acceptance: Invalid record retained in raw or quarantine.

challenges.title: Transformations, dimensional loading and SQL validation
challenges.scenario: Raw extracts need consistent labels, parsed dates and analytics-ready tables.
tasks: Inspect the normalisation logic in healthcare_etl_pipeline.py.
Review raw_encounters, raw_medication_orders, mart_encounters and mart_medication_orders.
Run the SQL audit queries.
Check uniqueness and referential integrity at the curated grain.
Document why missing costs are not replaced with zero.
challenges.starter:
sqlite3 assignments/outputs/healthcare_etl_training.db

Then execute sql/healthcare_etl/etl_audit_queries.sql in SQLite or DBeaver.
challenges.hint: A missing cost is unknown, not zero. Preserve NULL and exclude it from monetary totals unless an explicit imputation policy is approved.
challenges.solution: Use the SQL audit file to inspect run logs, mart grain, quality findings and left-join coverage. Confirm the encounter count and order count at their own grains. Never join raw order rows to encounter rows and then sum encounter-level metrics without deduplication.
challenges.expected: Curated encounter/order tables match source row counts when no records fail validation; foreign-reference exceptions are separated into quarantine.
acceptance: SQL totals reconcile to the ETL manifest.

challenges.title: Incremental loading, idempotency and run observability
challenges.scenario: The pipeline runs repeatedly. It must avoid duplicate records and provide a run history that helps an analyst troubleshoot failures.
tasks: Run the same source twice against the same SQLite database.
Compare mart counts and run log entries.
Explain the difference between append-only, replace/upsert and watermark-based incremental loads.
Identify why a timestamp watermark needs late-arriving data handling.
Propose run-level metrics: source rows, loaded rows, rejected rows, duration, status and checksum.
challenges.starter:
Current training pattern: INSERT OR REPLACE by primary key.
Production design considerations: updated_at watermark, overlap window, deduplication key, late-arriving events, transaction boundary and retry policy.
challenges.hint: Idempotency means repeating the same load does not create duplicate business records. It does not automatically solve changed records, deletes or late-arriving updates.
challenges.solution: Execute the pipeline twice. Mart counts should remain stable while `etl_run_log` records two distinct runs. Document a watermark design using a stable source `updated_at`, overlap window and deterministic upsert; do not implement a watermark on order_date alone if records can be corrected later.
challenges.expected: Stable curated counts across repeated identical runs and a distinct audit record per run.
acceptance: No claim that full CDC is implemented.

challenges.title: Scheduling, monitoring and operational handoff
challenges.scenario: A small analytics team needs a scheduled daily refresh and an understandable recovery procedure.
tasks: Review Linux systemd user timer and Windows Task Scheduler examples.
Configure a local schedule only after a successful manual run.
Inspect logs and manifests after scheduled execution.
Document failure alert, rerun, backup and retention steps.
Explain why a desktop user timer is not production orchestration.
challenges.starter:
Linux:
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now hda-etl.timer
systemctl --user list-timers

Windows: use the supplied `etl/windows` PowerShell instructions.
challenges.hint: First verify the script works manually. Scheduled tasks run with a different working directory and environment; use absolute paths and explicit interpreters.
challenges.solution: Follow `etl/systemd/README.md` on Linux or `etl/windows/README.md` on Windows. Confirm the timer points to the correct extracted folder. Inspect service logs and output manifests. Disable the timer when the exercise is complete.
challenges.expected: A documented local schedule with a successful run, visible logs and a tested disable procedure.

challenges.title: Timed end-to-end data pipeline assignment
challenges.scenario: A remote healthcare client requests a reproducible pipeline that loads a weekly encounter and medication-order extract into an analytics database and provides a concise quality report.
tasks: Create source inventory and data contracts.
Run CSV or mock API ingestion.
Validate keys, dates, quantities and references.
Transform and load curated tables.
Produce quality findings, manifest and SQL validation evidence.
Write a concise handoff with limitations and recovery steps.
challenges.starter:
100-point rubric:
Extraction and completeness 15
Data contracts and validation 20
Transformation and grain 15
Database load and idempotency 15
Logging, manifest and QA evidence 15
Security/privacy and limitations 10
Handoff and reproducibility 10
challenges.hint: A strong submission makes failure visible and traceable. Do not equate medication orders with dispensing or administration, and do not use real patient data in the exercise.
challenges.solution: Use the provided pipeline and audit SQL as the baseline. Include the run manifest, quality report, ETL run log, curated SQLite database, source checksums, a short README and a client handoff. Target ≥80/100; any silent row loss, duplicate key or untraceable failure requires remediation.
challenges.expected: A reproducible local pipeline with a complete audit trail and explicit synthetic-data caveats.
acceptance: Raw and curated layers are distinct.
Repeated run does not duplicate marts.
